segments.title: Opening: The Art of Social Engineering

utterances.text: Welcome to Miss Marjoribanks Unpacked, a close reading of one of Victorian fiction's most underrated masterpieces.
Mrs Oliphant published Miss Marjoribanks in 1866, and it has been quietly astonishing readers ever since.
It is a novel about a young woman who returns from school to her widowed father's house in a provincial town, and proceeds to reorganise every social arrangement within reach.
She does this with such total conviction and such devastating competence that you are never quite sure whether to admire her or be slightly afraid.
Joining me today are three readers who have thought long and hard about why this novel is so extraordinary.
Dr Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher who cares deeply about how fiction is actually built — the sentences, the architecture, the sleight of hand.
She is precisely the right reader for a novel this carefully engineered.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal and social historian who specialises in the real institutions behind the fiction — what the world of Carlingford actually looked like from the outside in.
He has the enviable gift of making the past feel immediate and, on occasion, genuinely alarming.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who first read Miss Marjoribanks as a teenager and has returned to it more times than she can count.
She brings the perspective of the dedicated reader — the one who notices what makes you stop and read a sentence twice.
I want to start where the novel itself starts — with the question of social engineering, and with Lucilla's almost breathtaking self-belief.
Eleanor, she is a remarkable creation from the very first pages. What does Oliphant do to make her so immediately compelling?
What Oliphant does — and she does it almost immediately — is give Lucilla a kind of psychological architecture that most novelists would spend three chapters establishing.
Lucilla's self-belief is not vanity in the ordinary sense. It's something stranger and more interesting — a genuine conviction that her own concerns are universally compelling.
The narrator spells it out with this wonderful surgical precision. The passage reads:

"Lucilla, for her part, had the calmest and most profound conviction that, when she discussed her own doings and plans and clevernesses, she was bringing forward the subject most interesting to her audience as well as to herself."
That word "clevernesses" is doing extraordinary work — it has this slightly comic, almost affectionate edge that keeps the satire from becoming cruel.
And then Oliphant adds one devastating sentence: "Such a conviction is never without its fruits."
That is the narrator stepping back and saying — she's right, you know. It works.
What strikes me about that passage — and Eleanor is quite right about its precision — is that it describes something we now have an entire vocabulary for in behavioural economics.
The projection of confidence as a mechanism of persuasion. Lucilla doesn't ask permission to be important — she simply assumes it, and the social world around her adjusts accordingly.
In 1866, for a young woman of Lucilla's station, that was not merely unusual. It was almost structurally impossible — and yet Oliphant makes it entirely credible.
Because the tools Lucilla deploys — the dinner parties, the drawing room entertainments — those were the only legitimate instruments available to her.
She is engineering a world within the only space she is legally permitted to occupy.
James's point about legitimate instruments is exactly it — but what gets me is the comedy of it.
Oliphant is laughing at Lucilla, gently. And then almost immediately siding with her. You feel both things at once.
The first time I read that passage about her "calmest and most profound conviction" I laughed out loud. And then I thought — but she's not wrong, is she?
People do find her the most interesting subject. The whole novel proves it.
That double register — the satire and the sympathy running simultaneously — is what makes Oliphant so technically remarkable.
And she extends it beautifully when she describes what Lucilla is actually working with — the social raw material of Carlingford.
There's this extraordinary passage — it's almost a single enormous sentence — cataloguing every element the town has to offer.

"When you add to a man capable of giving excellent dinners, like Dr Marjoribanks, another man like young Mr Cavendish... it will be plainly apparent that all that was wanting to Carlingford was a master-hand to blend these different elements."
"A master-hand to blend these different elements" — it's the language of cookery and of statecraft simultaneously.
Oliphant is equating what Lucilla does with genuine governance. And doing it with a completely straight face.
That catalogue is worth pausing on for a moment, because it's also a precise social map of a mid-Victorian provincial town.
You have the professional men — the doctor, the solicitors, the men who go out with the hounds when business permits.
You have the visiting classes — the barristers on circuit, the race-goers, the county visitors — who give the town its sense of connection to a wider world.
And the curates — Oliphant notes that Mr Bury changes his curates very often — which is a very dry joke about the Church's own social mechanics.
Oliphant knows exactly what each of these figures represents in the hierarchy. And she knows that Lucilla knows.
What I find irresistible about that passage is its sheer momentum — it just keeps accumulating, clause after clause after clause.
It mimics the experience of social life itself — this endless parade of people requiring management and placement and entertainment.
And when you finally reach the end — that single phrase, "a master-hand" — it lands with such relief. Yes. That's what's been missing.
Lucilla. Obviously. She was always going to arrive.
And the other thing Oliphant gives her — which is rarer still — is genuine strategic foresight.
It's not just confidence. Lucilla plans. She anticipates problems before they arrive.
Oliphant describes it as:
"that faculty of throwing herself into the future, and anticipating the difficulties of a position, which is so valuable to all who aspire to be leaders of mankind."
"Leaders of mankind" — not leaders of Carlingford society, not leaders of the drawing room. Mankind.
Oliphant is entirely serious about Lucilla's scale of ambition, even as she finds it comic. That tension is the engine of the whole novel.
"Leaders of mankind" is a phrase with a very specific nineteenth-century charge to it — it's the language of public life, of political aspiration.
In 1866, women were legally barred from virtually every arena in which that phrase would normally apply.
So when Oliphant applies it to Lucilla's management of a Thursday evening in Grange Lane, there is real irony in that. And also, I think, real anger.
It's one of those sentences that gets funnier and more pointed every time you read it. The more you know about Victorian women's lives, the harder it lands.
Lucilla has this gift, this extraordinary capacity — and the only theatre available to her is a provincial drawing room.
She fills it completely. But you can't help feeling that Oliphant knows she deserved a larger stage.
That question of scale — of what Lucilla does with the territory available to her — seems like exactly the right place to go next.
Because the more closely you read this novel, the more it becomes clear that Lucilla's dominion is not small at all — and that she exercises it with a precision that is almost unsettling.
We'll turn to Lucilla herself — to character and control — right after this.
We've been talking about how Oliphant engineers her social world — but at the centre of that world stands one extraordinary figure.
This segment, we turn to Lucilla herself: how she works, what drives her, and why she remains one of the most compelling characters in Victorian fiction.
I want to start with something that makes readers laugh and then immediately makes them uneasy.
Lucilla is caught by the matrons in what ought to be an awkward confession.
She's been charming the gentlemen, everyone knows it, and the proper thing would be to deny it or at least blush.
Instead she simply says — and Oliphant gives us this in direct speech, which is rare and deliberate —
"I never pretend I don't try to please them."
And the matrons are worsted.
They have no comeback, because the confession contains no vulnerability.
Lucilla has stripped out the shame the matrons expected to weaponise, and left them with nothing.
That move is so precise, isn't it — Oliphant gives Lucilla the moral high ground by having her refuse to play the game of denial at all.
But what I find even more technically fascinating is the narrative frame Oliphant builds around that moment.
Lucilla knows she's winning; she knows the matrons know it; and the narrator makes sure we know all of this simultaneously.
That layered awareness — character, rival, reader, narrator — all in a single paragraph: it's astonishing compression.
And then Oliphant says the real reason Lucilla works so hard is not personal advantage — it's for the good of the community.
The irony is wielded with such a light touch that you almost miss how devastating it is.
The phrase "community in general" is doing a great deal of work there, historically speaking.
In the 1860s, the language of civic duty and public improvement was almost exclusively reserved for men — philanthropists, municipal reformers, parish councillors.
For Lucilla to claim that vocabulary for what amounts to running a very successful Thursday evening — that is a quietly radical act.
She's not being ironic about her work; she genuinely believes it is of civic significance.
And the novel, at some level, agrees with her — which is rather unsettling if you think about it too carefully.
That's exactly what I mean when I say reading Lucilla is an experience of perpetual slight vertigo.
Because Oliphant keeps telling us not to be cynical about her.
There's a passage I find myself returning to again and again — it's the most direct statement of what Lucilla actually is.

"Policy had been constantly inspired and backed by nature in the measures Lucilla had taken for the organisation and welfare of her kingdom, and even what people took for the cleverest calculation was in reality a succession of happy instincts."
A succession of happy instincts.
That phrase does so much to defend Lucilla from the charge of cold-bloodedness.
She's not a schemer — she's a genius, and genius works differently.
The word "kingdom" is the tell, isn't it.
Oliphant uses it with absolute seriousness — Carlingford is Lucilla's political territory in any meaningful sense of the word.
And then there's the earlier passage about Barbara Lake — where Lucilla is accompanying her at the piano and pauses to applaud at precisely the right moment.
Oliphant calls it the management of enlightened despotism — which is one of the great comic phrases in the book.

"She knew by instinct what sort of clay the people were made of by whom she had to work, and gave them their reward with that liberality and discrimination which is the glory of enlightened despotism."
"Clay" — she sees her social material the way a sculptor does.
And yet it's simultaneously an act of generosity, even of love — she applauds Barbara because Barbara needs it, and Lucilla knows that.
"Enlightened despotism" is a very specific phrase in the eighteenth and nineteenth century.
It refers to absolute rulers — Frederick the Great, Catherine II — who believed they governed in the interests of their subjects, whether the subjects liked it or not.
The benevolence is real; the power is still total.
Oliphant is being extremely precise when she reaches for that comparison for a young woman running a dinner party in a provincial English town.
It's funny, yes — but it's also a genuine political analysis of how social power actually operates in confined domestic spaces.
And what strikes me is how Oliphant handles the question of Lucilla's motives directly — she almost anticipates the cynical reading and rebuts it.
She writes — and again this is direct address, which I find rather startling —

"People who like to discover the alloy which blends with all human motives, may suppose that Lucilla felt her own credit as the leader of society at stake, and would not admit that she had been duped. But this had in reality but a very small share in the matter."
"The alloy which blends with all human motives" — that's a brilliant formulation.
She's naming the reductive cynical impulse — the assumption that all virtue conceals self-interest — and then refusing to grant it.
Lucilla is permitted to be genuinely good at her work and genuinely motivated by something larger than ego.
In a Victorian novel, that is almost revolutionary.
It is revolutionary, and I think part of why is formal, not just thematic.
When Oliphant writes that phrase — "people who like to discover the alloy" — she's addressing an implied reader who wants to debunk Lucilla.
And by naming that reader's desire so precisely, she neutralises it.
Then there's that wonderful closing beat later in the same chapter — where the narrator steps back to render a verdict on Lucilla's progress.
"Lucilla was not blind to the dangers that surrounded her, nor indifferent to the partial disappointment she had undergone; but she saw that, in spite of all, her great work was making progress."
"And when we announce that Miss Marjoribanks herself was satisfied, there remains little more to say."
That "we" is doing so much.
The narrator allies herself with Lucilla's authority — as if the novel itself is Lucilla's kingdom.
That phrase — "her great work" — I keep circling back to it.
It's the language used in the period for engineering projects, for philanthropic institutions, for colonial administration.
Lucilla's social management of Carlingford gets the same weight as building a railway or founding a school.
The question the novel keeps asking, without quite answering, is whether that's satirical — or simply accurate.
And perhaps that ambiguity — whether Lucilla's work is satire or sincere tribute — is precisely what makes Oliphant such a rewarding novelist to sit with.
Coming up, we zoom out from Lucilla herself to look at the society she inhabits — and what Oliphant reveals when she turns her microscope on Carlingford as a whole.
We've been exploring how Lucilla shapes the people around her — but of course, that raises a larger question.
What kind of society is she actually operating in — and what does Oliphant think of it?
This is where the novel becomes genuinely interesting as a social document, not just a comic entertainment.
Oliphant opens her account of Carlingford with a diagnosis — and it is not a flattering one.
She sets up the premise of the whole novel with a single dry sentence.
That word — lamentable — is doing enormous work.
It is mock-heroic, yes, but it also carries a genuine edge of reproach.
There is real human material here, the narrator implies, going entirely to waste.
And that phrase, human material — it's the novelist's eye, isn't it?
Oliphant is watching society the way a sculptor watches a block of marble — assessing what could be made from it.
And then, hilariously, she gives us Lucilla as the sculptor.
The joke deepens when we see what Lucilla actually achieves — because the novel rewards her project, even as it mocks it.
There's that wonderful moment after her Thursday evenings begin drawing real crowds.
The mock-grandiosity is perfect — benefactors of the world, for organizing a drawing room.
And yet Oliphant won't quite let you dismiss it either.
What strikes me about that passage is the visual pay-off that follows it.
Oliphant first gives us all that commentary about ingratitude and critics — and then simply shows us the room.
She writes that the furniture is veiled and hidden by the robes of a radiant flood of society.
A radiant flood — it's almost biblical.
Society pours in and transforms the space, and Lucilla is vindicated without a word of argument.
But that radiant flood has very definite edges — it doesn't include everyone.
And Oliphant is quite precise about where those edges fall.
The passage describing Barbara Lake at one of these evenings is, I think, the most quietly devastating in the chapter.
Six times washed.
That is not a detail you put in by accident.
It tells you exactly how many times Barbara's family has been unable to afford a new dress.
The precision is the indictment.
It's also the emotional complexity of Barbara that gets me — fright and defiance at once.
She hasn't surrendered to her situation, but she's frightened by it.
And she is simultaneously inside the group — part of it by chance combination — and utterly outside it.
Oliphant holds both truths without resolving them, which is rare and rather wonderful.
That structural doubling — inside and outside, part of and apart from — it's central to how Oliphant builds her social critique.
She never lets the comedy of manners forget that manners have real victims.
And then, just when you think the satire is entirely gentle, something like the hanging remark arrives.
That exchange is startling even now.
An amusing man — Oliphant's designation, not mine — announces to the drawing room, quite casually:
As good as a play.
A man's death, offered as provincial entertainment — and no one in the room objects.
That silence is part of the indictment too.
And it connects to that extraordinary moment with the barrister — also in chapter seven.
He delivers his considered view — his judicial opinion, practically — on a certain class of criminal.
No soul.
Stated with complete solemnity, after many opportunities of observing.
Oliphant lets him hang himself entirely with his own syntax.
The legal resonance there is precise and intentional.
This is a barrister — a man trained to construct arguments about who deserves punishment.
And Oliphant places his theory of the soulless criminal class inside a drawing room conversation, on a Thursday evening, between the soup and the music.
The juxtaposition is the entire argument.
There's something almost Austenian about the technique — the polite surface that cannot quite contain the violence underneath.
But I think Oliphant is angrier than Austen — and more willing to let that anger show in the narrator's voice.
The omniscient narration in this novel has real claws.
That quality — the narrator's barely concealed impatience with Carlingford's complacency — runs through everything we've been discussing today.
And it's about to find a dramatic focal point — because the social machinery Lucilla has so carefully constructed is heading for a very particular collision.

segments.title: The Cavendish Rupture: Plot and Propriety

utterances.text: We've been looking at how Oliphant uses Carlingford's social rituals as a lens — and now we turn to the moment those rituals begin to crack.
The Cavendish storyline is where propriety stops being decorative and starts being lethal.
What strikes me first is how Oliphant sets up the machinery of rumour before the collapse even begins.
There's a passage early on about the nature of gossip in Grange Lane that is almost scientific in its precision.
"news had a wonderful tendency to increase and grow bigger as it spread in Grange Lane"
Cavendish is merely absent — and Carlingford inflates that absence into a dying friend, a probable inheritance, a reinvented fortune.
The community isn't malicious — it's imaginative, which is almost worse, because the fiction it constructs has no anchor in fact.
And Oliphant phrases it so beautifully — "a wonderful tendency."
That word "wonderful" is doing something sly — it's affectionate and damning at once.
Carlingford isn't being censured — it's being observed with this warm, clear-eyed amusement.
But underneath the comedy, there's a man whose entire identity depends on what that rumour-mill decides to believe about him.
That's precisely it — and Oliphant makes the stakes explicit in a later passage that I find genuinely haunting.
Cavendish reaches a moment of terrible clarity about what he values most.

"he could rather be content to lose them all at a stroke, to make it known in Carlingford that he was ruined and had lost his fortune, than that Carlingford should find out that he was not, after all, one of the Cavendishes"
Financial ruin is survivable — he could leave, reinvent himself, start again somewhere else.
But to be publicly unmasked as a fraud within the social order you've spent your life inhabiting — that is existential annihilation.
From a social historian's perspective, this captures something real about nineteenth-century provincial society — name was not merely reputation, it was ontology.
What I want to add to that is the way Oliphant engineers the ironic contrast in chapter twenty-nine — it's structural brilliance.
While Cavendish is agonising over his identity, Lucilla is quietly writing him a letter in her — and this is the phrase — "sacred retirement of her own maiden chamber, when all the world was still."
And at that same moment, General Travers is, as the narrator says, "chaffing" Cavendish about the beautiful and disinterested friendship which united him to the young sovereign of Grange Lane.
The simultaneity is the joke — and the point.
While men are posturing and chattering about Lucilla, she is already acting — she has written the letter.
Oliphant keeps staging these moments where female agency and male performance run parallel on the page — and the women are always three moves ahead.
The word "chaffing" in particular — Oliphant has the narrator note that this is how the General would "vulgarly" put it.
That little word "vulgarly" is doing enormous work — the narrator distances herself from the General's blokish register even while reporting it.
And it puts Lucilla and the narrator in the same superior position — both watching the men perform their social theatre.
But the pathos of Cavendish sharpens considerably when Oliphant returns to his past moments of triumph — and shows how hollow they were.
There's a passage in chapter forty-one where we see him walking the same path he once walked after the Archdeacon's defeat.
"when Mr Cavendish felt all the sweetness of being a member of an oligarchy, and entitled to the sympathy and support of his order"
And now — Oliphant gives us this devastating contrast — "he went along the same path with his hat over his ears and his hands in his pockets, and rage and pain in his heart."
The oligarchy gave him its sweetness only so long as he could perform membership convincingly — and he no longer can.
That is the real law of Grange Lane, more binding than anything on the statute books.
And then Oliphant drives the knife in further with that election eve scene — which is such controlled dramatic irony.
Oliphant itemises his self-destruction in this extraordinary triple repetition — "he who... he who... he who..."

"He was there—he who had been so long away from Carlingford—he who had been so deeply offended by hearing his name seriously coupled with that of Barbara Lake—he who ought to have been anywhere in the world rather than here upon the eve of his election"
Each "he who" clause adds another layer of self-contradiction — he knows exactly how wrong this is, and he does it anyway.
That rhetorical structure is Oliphant's way of making us feel the compulsion from the inside — it's not stupidity, it's something more helpless than that.
And then the punishment arrives with this perfect comic timing — as he comes out of the house, he walks straight into his chief Dissenting supporters.
The passage notes they stopped to speak to him "with a curiously critical air" — and he has to be, as the narrator puts it, "every man's friend for the time being."
The humiliation is total and entirely self-inflicted — and Oliphant delivers it without a single exclamation.
Just that dry little phrase — "as a matter of course" — before telling us he walked straight into them.
The Rector's response to all this is equally well observed — there's a passage in chapter forty-eight where the poor man is practically vibrating with thwarted rectitude.
He had staked his honour on Cavendish's repentance, and now Cavendish is — and I love this phrase —
"going back, publicly to wallow in the mire—and it was Sunday when such a worldly subject ought not to be permitted to enter a good man's mind"
The comedy is exquisite — the Rector can't act because it's Sunday, and the news is spreading precisely because Sunday has heightened the election excitement beyond all ordinary measure.
As Oliphant tells us — that Sunday was "a severer calamity for Mr Cavendish than half a dozen ordinary days."
The institution that should be protecting order — the Sabbath, the Church — becomes the mechanism of his destruction.
What emerges from all of this is Oliphant as a novelist who is simultaneously inside the comedy and coolly above it — laughing with her characters and at them in the same sentence.
Which brings us naturally to a question we've been circling — whose voice are we actually hearing when the narration speaks?
That distance, that irony, the way the narrator slides in and out of the characters' own assumptions — that's where we're heading next.
We've been talking about the fractures in Carlingford's social fabric — the rupture with the Cavendishes, the way propriety both governs and masks.
What I want to turn to now is the instrument that makes all of that visible: Oliphant's narration itself — the voice that watches Lucilla and never quite lets her off the hook.
That word — 'watches' — is exactly right, and it's worth sitting with, because the narrator's relationship to Lucilla is so singular.
It's not satirical distance in the cold Augustan sense — there's genuine warmth in it — but the narrator never loses the capacity to see through Lucilla completely.
There's a passage very early in the novel that establishes this with almost frightening precision.

"Dr Marjoribanks had no means of knowing that his daughter was only doing her duty by him in his widowhood, according to a programme of filial devotion resolved upon, in accordance with the best models, some days before."
The phrase 'programme of filial devotion' is almost breathtaking in its audacity.
Lucilla has scripted her grief before she has even experienced it — and the narrator tells us this with perfect composure, no exclamation mark, no moral judgment.
That restraint is the technique — the dryness is the point.
And I think the historical weight of 'best models' is doing enormous work there and shouldn't be underestimated.
Conduct literature for young women in the mid-Victorian period was an entire industry — prescriptive manuals, improving fiction, sermons on female duty in bereavement.
Lucilla has absorbed all of that and turned it into operational strategy.

What Oliphant's narrator is exposing is not that Lucilla is cold — she may not be — but that the prescribed forms of female feeling have become so codified that a sufficiently intelligent woman can simply deploy them.
Whether there is genuine feeling beneath the programme is a question the narrator declines to answer — and that silence is its own form of irony.
What strikes me, though, is that this ironic distance is never cruel.
And there's a scene in Chapter Sixteen that shows the other side of it — where the comedy is genuinely delightful, and the narrator's position shifts almost imperceptibly.
Lucilla has manoeuvred the cook Nancy into making some special dish by pretending to be in low spirits.
And she recounts it at the dinner table with this gorgeous, guileless satisfaction.
"I could not think how I was going to get her to consent, but you know she thought I was in low spirits, the dear old soul, and that it would be a comfort to me."
'The dear old soul' — she says it with such affection, and she has just confessed to a small manipulation in the same breath.
That is the comedy, and it is warm — it is not mockery.
And the narrator catches the social response to that moment with equal precision.
Because what follows is not just laughter — the whole table has been caught out.
"The laughter was not mere laughter, but conveyed, at the same time a confession of guilt and a storm of applause and admiration."
'A confession of guilt' — they had all been speculating about Lucilla's distress, and Lucilla has turned the tables and made it a dinner-party entertainment.
The narrator has to do three things at once in that sentence: report a social event, anatomise an emotional response, and deliver a moral verdict.
And she does it in a single subordinate clause.
There's something worth dwelling on in the structure of that guilt, though.
The company has been watching for signs of female collapse — they expected Lucilla to perform distress, and they were ready to assess it.
The social ritual of speculating about a young woman's emotional state after a romantic disappointment — that is a very specific Victorian institution.
And Lucilla defeats it entirely by simply refusing to perform the expected feeling.
The applause is real — she has won — but what she has won against is a system of surveillance.
And this is where Oliphant complicates her heroine in a way I find endlessly interesting.
Because Lucilla is genuinely formidable — she outmanoeuvres everyone — and yet the narrator gives us this extraordinary aside about her limitations.
She lacks a sense of humour.
She can use Mrs Woodburn's gift for mimicry as an instrument, but she cannot feel why it is funny.
And the way Oliphant phrases it is absolutely characteristic — not unkind, but absolutely precise.
"Lucilla had no sense of humour, as she candidly admitted, with that consciousness of her own faults, and slight disposition to consider them virtues, which is common to persons of great endowments."
'A slight disposition to consider them virtues' — that is such a precise skewer.
Lucilla knows her faults — and she has basically decided they don't matter, which they don't, because she is right about almost everything else.
That passage is also doing something structurally important by placing Lucilla and Mrs Woodburn in direct comparison.
Mrs Woodburn has a singular talent — the mimicry is dazzling — but she is, as the narrator drily notes, a little indolent.
Lucilla has no such talent and no such indolence — she has what the narrator calls, with a perfectly straight face, 'genius.'
Oliphant gives that word to Lucilla's organisational power over Carlingford social life — and she means it.
The irony is that the narrator is completely sincere in calling it genius, and that is what makes the whole novel shimmer.
Which brings us back to the narrator's structural position, in a sense.
The voice never condescends to Lucilla — it holds her at arm's length precisely because it respects what she is doing.
And yet it refuses to pretend that what she is doing is anything other than what it is: the management of a constrained life through exceptional intelligence.
The irony is protective of Lucilla as much as it is diagnostic.
Protective irony — that is a phrase worth keeping.
A narrator who sees everything and judges sparingly — and uses that restraint as a form of solidarity.
That solidarity is about to face a serious test, because someone is returning to Carlingford who will throw Lucilla's composure — and the novel's tone — into genuine uncertainty.
We've been exploring how Oliphant's ironic narration keeps us at a careful, knowing distance from her characters.
But in this segment, we're going to see what happens when the plot forces its way through that irony — when desire and disruption arrive in the shape of Tom Marjoribanks.
Tom's return is one of the great structural surprises of the novel, and I think it catches even seasoned readers off guard.
We've been given ten years of Lucilla in total command — of Grange Lane, of Thursday evenings, of every social situation she enters.
And then Tom walks back through the door, and the narration does something quite extraordinary.
Lucilla reaches out her hands to welcome him — she's poised, she's composed, she's entirely Lucilla.

"she found herself, before she knew how, in the arms of a man with a beard, who was so much changed in his own person that he ventured to kiss her, which was a thing Tom Marjoribanks, though her cousin, had never dared to do before."
That phrase — 'before she knew how' — is doing so much work.
Lucilla always knows how. That's her defining characteristic. And for one moment, she doesn't.
What strikes me every time I read that passage is the beard.
It sounds almost comic, and it is — but it's also genuinely unsettling for Lucilla.
The beard is the physical sign that the world has moved on while she's been arranging things in Carlingford.
Tom has gone to India, grown a beard, become — Oliphant's word — a man.
And the kiss is the punctuation mark on all of that.
It signals that the old rules — the ones Lucilla set — no longer apply quite as neatly as they did.
There's a legal and social dimension to that kiss that I think modern readers can miss.
Tom is her cousin — a first cousin — and in Victorian England, first-cousin marriage was not only legal but common, even respectable.
So the narrator's note that he had 'never dared' to kiss her before is a small but pointed social signal.
He always had the theoretical right to press his suit. Lucilla simply hadn't permitted it.
Which is entirely consistent with what we see earlier in the novel — where Tom obeys Lucilla rather than her father.
The Doctor himself watches this with what the narrator calls 'a little amazement and a little amusement.'

"recognising, with something of the surprise which that discovery always gives to fathers and mothers, that his visitor cared twenty times more for what Lucilla said than for anything that his superior wisdom could suggest."
'Superior wisdom' — delivered with barely concealed irony. Oliphant is very dry about paternal authority.
And the early Tom — the one who obeys Lucilla over the Doctor — is already the template for the returning Tom.
What's changed isn't his devotion. It's his willingness to act on it without asking permission.
And he says so directly. The passage where he declares himself is remarkable for its plainness.
"There never was a time that I would not have gone to the other end of the world if you had told me; and I have done it as near as possible."
That 'as near as possible' is a masterstroke.
It's funny, it's self-deprecating, and it's completely sincere all at once.
Tom is not an eloquent man. But he is, at this moment, devastating.
I always feel for Lucilla in that moment, which is not a feeling she typically invites.
She's spent the novel being the most clear-sighted person in every room.
And here is Tom — dear blundering Tom — seeing straight to the centre of everything.
Oliphant's line about it is one I come back to again and again.
"Blunderer as he was, he had gone direct to the very heart of the question, and it was impossible not to tremble a little in the presence of such straightforward clear-sightedness."
'Tremble a little.' That's the phrase that gets me every time.
Lucilla doesn't collapse. She doesn't swoon. She trembles — just a little.
And then she sits back down, because she has no idea what to do next.
It's worth dwelling on how unusual that moment is in the novel's economy.
Lucilla has managed nearly every situation she's encountered — often by sheer force of organised cheerfulness.
But Tom's question — 'him or you?' — is one that Lucilla's social machinery can't simply process and redirect.
Because it's asking her to choose between her own desire and the role she's constructed for herself.
And that is, in many ways, the question the entire novel has been building toward.
Absolutely. And Oliphant's genius is that she makes us unsure whether Lucilla knows the answer herself.
The sitting back down — that physical beat — is doing the work that a lesser novelist would do with three paragraphs of interior monologue.
Oliphant trusts the gesture. She trusts us. That's craft.
And that question — what Lucilla chooses, and what she must surrender to choose it — is precisely where we're headed next.
We'll be looking at the limits of female authority in the novel — and what Oliphant finally allows her heroine to have.

segments.title: Closing: The Limits of Female Authority

utterances.text: We've been talking about desire and disruption — Tom's return and what it unsettles in Lucilla's carefully constructed world.
But I want to end by stepping back and asking a larger question: what are the actual limits of Lucilla's authority — and what does Oliphant think about them?
There's a passage that cuts right to the heart of this, and I keep coming back to it.
After her father goes back downstairs to write his piece for the Lancet, Oliphant gives us this extraordinary interior moment.
"Lucilla passed through one of those moments of sublime despondency which now and then try the spirits of the benefactors of their race."
"Benefactors of their race" — Oliphant isn't mocking Lucilla, not entirely.
She's holding two things simultaneously: the comedy of Lucilla's grandiosity, and something genuinely tragic about a woman whose ambitions have nowhere adequate to go.
The tears are real, even if the framing is ironic.
That phrase does something quite specific to the reader, doesn't it.
"Sublime despondency" — the adjective is enormous, Miltonic almost, and it's attached to a woman sitting alone in a drawing room crying because people won't cooperate with her social vision.
But here's what gets me on every re-read: Oliphant adds that without such trials, genius would not fully know itself.
She's applying the logic of heroic suffering — the language we'd use for Napoleon or Milton — to a Victorian woman managing dinner parties.
It's funny and it's also a quiet indictment of a world that made the drawing room the only arena available.
And yet Lucilla doesn't leave the arena.
That's the thing historians tend to notice — the options actually available to women of her class and moment when life didn't go as planned.
Oliphant catalogues them with wonderful contempt: marriage tours, foreign travel, going out as a governess.
These are the escape hatches, and the narrator dismisses them as the resort of people who, and I'm quoting directly here, "know no better."
"But as for Miss Marjoribanks, she stood bravely at her post, and scorned to flinch or run away."
"Thus commenced, amid mists of discouragement, and in an entire absence of all that was calculated to stimulate and exhilarate, the second grand period of Lucilla's life."
The military language — "stood at her post," "scorned to flinch" — is doing real work.
Oliphant is insisting that staying put and continuing to work, in the face of failure and without applause, is genuine courage.
And that insistence runs right up against the novel's central structural irony — which is that the sphere Lucilla refuses to abandon is also the sphere that cannot fully contain her.
Oliphant states it almost baldly in one of the later chapters.
"When a woman happens to be full of energy and spirit, and determined that whatever she may be she shall certainly not be a nonentity, her position is one that demands thought."
"Demands thought" — that's the narrator refusing to resolve the dilemma.
It's not a program, it's not a solution — it's an acknowledgment that the problem is real and the world hasn't caught up.
What strikes me in that passage is the phrase "certainly not be a nonentity."
It's such a negative formulation — not "she wants to be great" or "she wants power," but she refuses to be nothing.
And that feels very true to how female ambition actually had to express itself — not as a claim to something, but as a refusal to disappear.
Lucilla never gets to say what she's actually for, only what she won't be.
That's the bind Oliphant maps so precisely, and it's not one that resolved itself quickly — in life or in literature.
Lucilla has no vocation in the religious sense, the narrator tells us plainly — no calling that would justify total self-abnegation.
But she also can't simply dissolve herself into the service of others the way the culture around her suggests she should.
The unresolved ethical dilemma isn't a failure of the novel — it's a faithful record of the actual historical impasse women like Lucilla faced.
And Oliphant refuses the consoling ending — or rather, she gives Lucilla the conventional ending, marriage and the estate, and then insists on the ambivalence anyway.
Lucilla's authority doesn't evaporate when she marries — but it does change shape, and Oliphant is careful not to pretend that's simple or cost-free.
The novel holds the irony and the admiration right to the end, and that's what makes it so remarkable.
I think that's the perfect note to end on — a novel that neither flinches from Lucilla's limitations nor underestimates her achievement.
My warmest thanks to Eleanor Hartley, James Blackstone, and Caroline Woodcourt — three readers who have made this novel feel both larger and more alive.
We've moved through Lucilla's ambitions and her social campaigns, through the comedy and the pathos of a woman who genuinely believes she is a benefactor of her race.
And we've seen how Mrs Oliphant holds the irony and the admiration together without blinking.
If you haven't read Miss Marjoribanks, I hope today has sent you straight to it.
And if you have, I suspect you'll be re-reading certain passages before the week is out.
Thank you for listening to Miss Marjoribanks Unpacked.

c2:p15.text:
There are people who talk of
themselves, and think of themselves, as it were, under protest, and with
depreciation, not actually able to convince themselves that anybody
cares; but Lucilla, for her part, had the calmest and most profound
conviction that, when she discussed her own doings and plans and
clevernesses, she was bringing forward the subject most interesting to
her audience as well as to herself. Such a conviction is never without
its fruits.
c2:p15.summary: Lucilla's complete conviction in her own importance is the source of her persuasiveness; she genuinely believes her interests are everyone's interests.

c3:p16.text:
When you add to a man capable of giving excellent dinners,
like Dr Marjoribanks, another man like young Mr Cavendish, Mrs
Woodburn's brother, who was a wit and a man of fashion, and belonged to
one of the best clubs in town, and brought down gossip with the bloom on
it to Grange Lane; and when you join to Mrs Centum, who was always so
good and so much out of temper that it was safe to calculate on
something amusing from her, the languid but trenchant humour of Mrs
Woodburn—not to speak of their husbands, who were perfectly available
for the background, and all the nephews and cousins and grand-children,
who constantly paid visits to old Mr Western and Colonel Chiley; and the
Browns, when they were at home, with their floating suite of admirers;
and the young ladies who sang, and the young ladies who sketched, and
the men who went out with the hounds, when business permitted them; and
the people who came about the town when there was an election; and the
barristers who made the circuit; and the gay people who came to the
races; not to speak of the varying chances of curates, who could talk or
play the piano, with which Mr Bury favoured his parishioners—for he
changed his curates very often; and the occasional visits of the lesser
county people, and the country clergymen;—it will be plainly apparent
that all that was wanting to Carlingford was a master-hand to blend
these different elements.
c3:p16.summary: The narrator catalogs Carlingford's abundant social assets—excellent dinners, witty figures, entertaining women, visiting relatives, local events, clergy, and county visitors—requiring only masterful coordination.
c3:p16.best_quote: all that was wanting to Carlingford was a master-hand to blend these different elements

c5:p36.text:
Nothing, indeed, could have come more
opportunely for Lucilla, who possessed in perfection that faculty of
throwing herself into the future, and anticipating the difficulties of a
position, which is so valuable to all who aspire to be leaders of
mankind.
c5:p36.summary: Lucilla possesses the valuable ability to anticipate difficulties and plan ahead, a trait essential for leadership.
c5:p36.best_quote: that faculty of throwing herself into the future, and anticipating the difficulties of a position, which is so valuable to all who aspire to be leaders of mankind

c13:p5.text:
And Lucilla knew it just as well as they
did, which gave a certain sense of condescension and superiority to her
frankness. "I never pretend I don't try to please them," Miss
Marjoribanks said; and the matrons found themselves worsted as usual;
for, to be sure, it was not for  Them , but for the good of the
community in general, that Lucilla exerted herself so successfully.
c13:p5.summary: Lucilla frankly states she makes no pretence of not trying to please gentlemen, leaving the matrons defeated, as her efforts serve community good rather than personal interest.
c13:p5.best_quote: I never pretend I don't try to please them

c14:p3.text:
Policy had been constantly inspired and backed by nature in
the measures Lucilla had taken for the organisation and welfare of her
kingdom, and even what people took for the cleverest calculation was in
reality a succession of happy instincts, by means of which, with the
sovereignty of true genius, Miss Marjoribanks managed to please
everybody by having her own way.
c14:p3.summary: Lucilla's success derives not from cold calculation but from happy instincts and true genius that blend policy with natural feeling.
c14:p3.best_quote: Policy had been constantly inspired and backed by nature in the measures Lucilla had taken for the organisation and welfare of her kingdom

c5:p18.text:
She paused a moment in the
accompaniment to clap her hands after that strophe was accomplished, and
then resumed with energy. For, to be sure, she knew by instinct what
sort of clay the people were made of by whom she had to work, and gave
them their reward with that liberality and discrimination which is the
glory of enlightened despotism. Miss Marjoribanks was naturally elated
when she had performed this important and successful  tour .
c5:p18.summary: Lucilla pauses to applaud Barbara's performance, understanding instinctively how to motivate people and dispense rewards with the discrimination of enlightened despotism.

c18:p47.text:
People who like to discover the alloy which blends
with all human motives, may suppose that Lucilla felt her own credit as
the leader of society at stake, and would not admit that she had been
duped. But this had in reality but a very small share in the matter.
c18:p47.summary: While others might suppose Lucilla's self-interest drives her actions, Oliphant asserts that reputation concerns play only a minor role in her character.
c18:p47.best_quote: People who like to discover the alloy which blends with all human motives, may suppose that Lucilla felt her own credit as the leader of society at stake, and would not admit that she had been duped. But this had in reality but a very small share in the matter.

c18:p66.text:
Lucilla
was not blind to the dangers that surrounded her, nor indifferent to the
partial disappointment she had undergone; but she saw that, in spite of
all, her great work was making progress. And when we announce that Miss
Marjoribanks herself was satisfied, there remains little more to say.
c18:p66.summary: Despite obstacles and disappointments, Lucilla recognizes that her great social work is advancing, and her satisfaction indicates victory.

And when we announce that Miss Marjoribanks herself was satisfied, there remains little more to say.

c3:p14.text:
Such was the
lamentable condition, at the moment this history commences, of society
in Carlingford.
c3:p14.summary: The narrator summarizes the deplorable state of Carlingford society at the start of the novel, despite abundant human material available for organizing.
c3:p14.best_quote: Such was the lamentable condition, at the moment this history commences, of society in Carlingford.

c10:p47.text:
Such, it is true, were the comments that were made upon the
public-spirited young woman who was doing so much for Carlingford; but
then Lucilla only shared the fate of all the great benefactors of the
world. An hour later the glories of the furniture were veiled and hidden
by the robes of a radiant flood of society, embracing all that was most
fair and all that was most distinguished in Carlingford.
c10:p47.summary: The narrator notes that Lucilla shares the common fate of great benefactors: criticism; an hour later the drawing-room is radiant with assembled society.
c10:p47.best_quote: Lucilla only shared the fate of all the great benefactors of the world

c10:p60.text:
Barbara's muslin, six times
washed, was not more different from the spotless lightness of all the
draperies round her, than was her air of fright, and at the same time of
defiance, from the gay babble and pleasant looks of the group which, by
a chance combination, she seemed to form part of.
c10:p60.summary: The narrator starkly contrasts Barbara's six-times-washed muslin with the pristine draperies around her, and her frightened defiance with the group's gaiety.

c7:p39.text:
"I think they are going to hang that
fellow that killed the tailor," said the amusing man; "that will stir
you up a little in Carlingford, I should suppose. It is as good as a
play for a country town.
c7:p39.summary: The guest mentions an upcoming execution of a man who killed a tailor and predicts it will provide entertainment for Carlingford's provincial society.
c7:p39.best_quote: I think they are going to hang that fellow that killed the tailor.

c7:p43.text:
It is a conclusion I have come to not rashly, but after many
opportunities of observing," the young man went on with solemnity; "on
the whole, my opinion is, that this is the great difference between one
portion of mankind and the other: that description of being, you may
take my word for it, has no soul."
c7:p43.summary: The barrister defends his position by claiming it is based on careful observation and represents the fundamental division in humanity between those with and without souls.
c7:p43.best_quote: this is the great difference between one portion of mankind and the other: that description of being, you may take my word for it, has no soul.

c22:p7.text:
As for Mr
Cavendish himself, it began to be understood that he was with a friend
who was sick, on the Continent; and soon—for news had a wonderful
tendency to increase and grow bigger as it spread in Grange Lane—that
his friend was dying, and that a probable large increase of fortune to
the popular favourite would be the result, which was an idea that did
credit to the imagination of Carlingford.
c22:p7.summary: Gossip about Mr Cavendish's absence spreads wildly, with rumours growing from a friend visiting him on the Continent to the friend dying and Cavendish inheriting a fortune.
c22:p7.best_quote: news had a wonderful tendency to increase and grow bigger as it spread in Grange Lane

c29:p45.text:
He had been doing without them
for a week or two, and he had not liked it; and yet at that moment it
seemed to Mr Cavendish that he could rather be content to lose them all
at a stroke, to make it known in Carlingford that he was ruined and had
lost his fortune, than that Carlingford should find out that he was not,
after all, one of the Cavendishes, nor the person it took him for.
c29:p45.summary: Cavendish realizes he would rather be financially ruined than exposed as a fraud, revealing his desperate attachment to social position.
c29:p45.best_quote: he could rather be content to lose them all at a stroke, to make it known in Carlingford that he was ruined and had lost his fortune, than that Carlingford should find out that he was not, after all, one of the Cavendishes

c29:p62.text:
It was with this
view that Miss Marjoribanks took the step of writing to Mr Cavendish. She had written in the sacred retirement of her own maiden chamber, when
all the world was still; perhaps at the moment when General Travers was,
as he would himself have vulgarly called it, "chaffing" Cavendish about
the beautiful and disinterested friendship which united him to the young
sovereign of Grange Lane.
c29:p62.summary: Lucilla writes her serious note while the General speaks about Cavendish and her, creating ironic contrast between her agency and male gossip.

c41:p22.text:
It
was after the Archdeacon had broken down in his case against the man
whom he called an adventurer, and when Mr Cavendish felt all the
sweetness of being a member of an oligarchy, and entitled to the
sympathy and support of his order. Now he went along the same path with
his hat over his ears and his hands in his pockets, and rage and pain in
his heart.
c41:p22.summary: The narrator recalls how Cavendish previously basked in oligarchic privilege after the Archdeacon's courtroom defeat, contrasting with his current isolation.
c41:p22.best_quote: when Mr Cavendish felt all the sweetness of being a member of an oligarchy, and entitled to the sympathy and support of his order

c47:p28.text:
He
was there—he who had been so long away from Carlingford—he who had
been so deeply offended by hearing his name seriously coupled with that
of Barbara Lake—he who ought to have been anywhere in the world rather
than here upon the eve of his election, when all the world was keeping
watch over his conduct.
c47:p28.summary: Cavendish's presence in Barbara's parlour two days before the election represents a catastrophic breach of propriety and political judgment.
c47:p28.best_quote: He was there—he who had been so long away from Carlingford—he who had been so deeply offended by hearing his name seriously coupled with that of Barbara Lake—he who ought to have been anywhere in the world rather than here upon the eve of his election, when all the world was keeping watch over his conduct.

c47:p56.text:
When he was
coming out of the house, as a matter of course, he met with the chief of
his Dissenting supporters, accompanied (for Mr Bury, as has been said,
was very Low-Church, and loved, wherever he could do it, to work in
unison with his Dissenting brethren) by the Rector's churchwarden, both
of whom stopped with a curiously critical air to speak to the Candidate,
who had to be every man's friend for the time being.
c47:p56.summary: Cavendish encounters his key supporters leaving the Lake house, and their critical looks suggest they have observed and judged his visit.

c48:p21.text:
He had staked his honour upon Mr Cavendish's
repentance, and here was he going back, publicly to wallow in the
mire—and it was Sunday when such a worldly subject ought not to be
permitted to enter a good man's mind, much less to be discussed and
acted upon as it ought to be if anything was to be done; for there was
little more than this sacred day remaining in which to undo the mischief
which a too great confidence in human nature had wrought.
c48:p21.summary: The Rector witnesses Cavendish's apparent backsliding just as Sunday prevents proper remedial action; his confidence in human nature proves false.
c48:p21.best_quote: here was he going back, publicly to wallow in the mire—and it was Sunday when such a worldly subject ought not to be permitted to enter a good man's mind

c48:p2.text:
This had been a comfort
to his mind, but it was the very falsest and most deceitful consolation. That intervening Sunday was a severer calamity for Mr Cavendish than
half a dozen ordinary days. The general excitement had risen so high,
and all the chances on both sides had been so often discussed and
debated, that something new was as water in the desert to the thirsting
constituency.
c48:p2.summary: The heightened election excitement makes Sunday a worse day for secrecy than any ordinary day; the news spreads like water in a desert.
c48:p2.best_quote: That intervening Sunday was a severer calamity for Mr Cavendish than half a dozen ordinary days.

c1:p46.text:
Lucilla was, it is true, as different from her mother
as summer from winter; but Dr Marjoribanks had no means of knowing that
his daughter was only doing her duty by him in his widowhood, according
to a programme of filial devotion resolved upon, in accordance with the
best models, some days before.

c1:p46.best_quote: Dr Marjoribanks had no means of knowing that his daughter was only doing her duty by him in his widowhood, according to a programme of filial devotion resolved upon, in accordance with the best models, some days before.

c16:p13.text:
"I could not think how
I was going to get her to consent," Lucilla said, "but you know she
thought I was in low spirits, the dear old soul, and that it would be a
comfort to me." Though there was often a great deal of fun at Dr
Marjoribanks's table, nothing was ever heard there to compare with the
laughter that greeted Lucilla's narrative.
c16:p13.summary: Lucilla reveals that she persuaded Nancy to prepare a special dish by claiming she was in low spirits, causing uproarious laughter.
c16:p13.best_quote: I could not think how I was going to get her to consent, but you know she thought I was in low spirits, the dear old soul, and that it would be a comfort to me

c16:p14.text:
Everybody was so entirely
aware of the supposed cause of the low spirits, and indeed was so
conscious of having speculated, like Nancy, upon Miss Marjoribanks's
probable demeanour at this trying moment, that the laughter was not mere
laughter, but conveyed, at the same time a confession of guilt and a
storm of applause and admiration.
c16:p14.summary: The narrator explains that the laughter is layered: it reveals the company's awareness of having speculated about Lucilla's distress and their amazement at her composure.
c16:p14.best_quote: the laughter was not mere laughter, but conveyed, at the same time a confession of guilt and a storm of applause and admiration

c25:p2.text:
The mimic was a little indolent, and would not take the trouble
to make any exertions for the good of the community, except in the
exercise of her peculiar talent, though she had been known, when
excited, to go through real fatigue for that; but she had none of the
steady force, the persevering energy—or, to sum up all in one word, the
genius—of Miss Marjoribanks, who, for her part, recognised the  use  of
such an instrument of entertainment as Mrs Woodburn possessed without
appreciating it in her own person; for Lucilla had no sense of humour,
as she candidly admitted, with that consciousness of her own faults, and
slight disposition to consider them virtues, which is common to persons
of great endowments.
c25:p2.summary: The narrator elaborates the fundamental difference: Mrs Woodburn relies on mimicry and entertainment talent, while Lucilla possesses steady organisational force, though Lucilla lacks humour despite her other gifts.
c25:p2.best_quote: Lucilla had no sense of humour, as she candidly admitted, with that consciousness of her own faults, and slight disposition to consider them virtues, which is common to persons of great endowments.

c50:p10.text:
She even had the strength to get up to meet him, and hold
out her hands to him by way of welcome—but found herself, before she
knew how, in the arms of a man with a beard, who was so much changed in
his own person that he ventured to kiss her, which was a thing Tom
Marjoribanks, though her cousin, had never dared to do before.
c50:p10.summary: Lucilla rises to greet Tom but finds herself embraced by a bearded, transformed man who dares to kiss her.
c50:p10.best_quote: she found herself, before she knew how, in the arms of a man with a beard, who was so much changed in his own person that he ventured to kiss her, which was a thing Tom Marjoribanks, though her cousin, had never dared to do before.

c6:p51.text:
These words, however, were addressed to deaf ears. Tom, as was natural,
had started immediately to obey Lucilla, as he was in duty bound; and
the old Doctor looked on with a little amazement and a little amusement,
recognising, with something of the surprise which that discovery always
gives to fathers and mothers, that his visitor cared twenty times more
for what Lucilla said than for anything that his superior wisdom could
suggest.
c6:p51.summary: Tom immediately obeys Lucilla instead of the Doctor, demonstrating that he values Lucilla's authority more than the Doctor's.
c6:p51.best_quote: recognising, with something of the surprise which that discovery always gives to fathers and mothers, that his visitor cared twenty times more for what Lucilla said than for anything that his superior wisdom could suggest.

c50:p23.text:
"Lucilla," said Tom Marjoribanks, "you know I always had a great regard
for my uncle. But it was not for him I came back. He was never half so
fond of me as I am of you. You know that as well as I do. There never
was a time that I would not have gone to the other end of the world if
you had told me; and I have done it as near as possible.
c50:p23.summary: Tom declares his deep regard for Lucilla has always exceeded his regard for her father, and that he left for India at her behest.
c50:p23.best_quote: There never was a time that I would not have gone to the other end of the world if you had told me; and I have done it as near as possible.

c50:p31.text:
"Him—or you!" said Lucilla, in dismay. Blunderer as he was, he had gone
direct to the very heart of the question, and it was impossible not to
tremble a little in the presence of such straightforward
clear-sightedness. Miss Marjoribanks had risen up to make her escape as
soon as it should be possible, but she was so much struck by Tom's
unlooked-for perspicuity, that she sat down again in her consternation.
c50:p31.summary: Lucilla is struck by Tom's unexpected perspicuity and forced to confront the central question; she sits down again, shaken by his clarity.
c50:p31.best_quote: Blunderer as he was, he had gone direct to the very heart of the question, and it was impossible not to tremble a little in the presence of such straightforward clear-sightedness.

c27:p57.text:
When Dr
Marjoribanks had gone downstairs to resume the case which he was writing
out for the  Lancet , Lucilla passed through one of those moments of
sublime despondency which now and then try the spirits of the
benefactors of their race. A few tears came to her eyes as she reflected
upon this great problem. Without such trials genius would not fully know
itself nor be justly aware of its own strength.
c27:p57.summary: Lucilla is moved to tears as she contemplates the problem of her unbelieving followers; without trials genius would not know its own strength.
c27:p57.best_quote: Lucilla passed through one of those moments of sublime despondency which now and then try the spirits of the benefactors of their race.

c36:p22.text:
People who know no better may go
away upon marriage tours, or they may fly off to foreign travel, or go
out as governesses, when all things do not go just as they wish. But as
for Miss Marjoribanks, she stood bravely at her post, and scorned to
flinch or run away. Thus commenced, amid mists of discouragement, and in
an entire absence of all that was calculated to stimulate and
exhilarate, the second grand period of Lucilla's life.
c36:p22.summary: While lesser people flee through marriage, travel, or governessing when disappointed, Lucilla stands firm at her post and begins her second campaign amid discouragement and without support.
c36:p22.best_quote: But as for Miss Marjoribanks, she stood bravely at her post, and scorned to flinch or run away. Thus commenced, amid mists of discouragement, and in an entire absence of all that was calculated to stimulate and exhilarate, the second grand period of Lucilla's life.

c46:p43.text:
She had
no vocation, such as the foundress of such an establishment ought to
have, nor did she see her way to the abandonment of all projects for
herself, and that utter devotion to the cause of humanity which would be
involved in it; but yet, when a woman happens to be full of energy and
spirit, and determined that whatever she may be she shall certainly not
be a nonentity, her position is one that demands thought.
c46:p43.summary: Lucilla lacks true religious vocation but will not surrender personal ambition; her energetic temperament creates an unresolved ethical dilemma.
c46:p43.best_quote: but yet, when a woman happens to be full of energy and spirit, and determined that whatever she may be she shall certainly not be a nonentity, her position is one that demands thought
